newsitem.title: UK: Oil to stay firm despite lower Iraqi premium.
newsitem.headline: Oil to stay firm despite lower Iraqi premium.

text.p: Oil prices are poised to stay firm for the rest of the year even if the military confrontation between Iraq and the United States is defused, thanks to bullish supply-demand fundamentals, traders said on Wednesday.

Lingering concerns over tight heating oil stocks approaching the northern winter and an indefinite delay to the United Nation's Iraqi oil-for-food arrangement should keep world benchmark North Sea Brent blend over $20 a barrel for the next few weeks.
And oil prices should continue to incorporate a small premium to allow for Middle East instability, the traders said.
Brent futures on Tuesday morning in London were trading at $22.10, off last week's post-Gulf War high of $24.37 but still some $6 over price levels at this time last year.

"It's a fairly strong market and heating oil looks good going into winter," said Jeff Potter, managing director of brokers Univest Ireland in Dublin. "Technically it looks great. I think $21.50 should hold for the time being."

"I think given the fact on August 30 we were at $21, I think this is where the market is going to look to stabilize," at $21 to $21.60, said David Oxley, an oil trader at Credit Lyonnais Rouse in London.
"There is still underlying tension (in the Middle East) so a 60-cent premium on the back of that tension is not that big of a deal," he said.
The U.S. State Department said on Tuesday it had sent a fresh message to Iraq telling it not to interfere with Western enforcement of no-fly zones.

When U.S. missiles attacked Iraq two weeks ago in retaliation for an Iraqi move against Kurds in the north, it put on indefinite hold a United Nations plan allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months.
That robbed the market of about 600,000-700,000 barrels per day of oil that refiners were counting on to meet demand for heating oil ahead of winter.
"The loss of anticipated Iraqi oil exports creates an unexpected problem for the oil market," said the Centre for Global Energy Studies in London.
"Instead of worrying about potential oversupply and weaker prices during the fourth quarter the industry is now preoccupied with possible supply shortages and higher prices."
Gulf oil and OPEC sources said on Tuesday that OPEC members were not rushing to cash in on the unexpected oil price bonanza by increasing the group's oil production.
"We've probably taken a majority of the premium out of the market but it is still unclear if a new trend is developing," said Leslie Nicholas, energy analyst at GNI Ltd in London.

"If we see distillate inventory builds continuing then further losses are probable," he said. "At the current moment somewhere in the region of $20 reflects current fundamentals for me unless we see more bullishness in the products."
Analysts pointed to low distillate inventories on both sides of the Atlantic and a strong demand for barge deliveries to northern European buyers, particularly Germany.
Middle distillate stocks in Europe rose 3.75 million barrels in August from July to 286.28 million, but are 25.8 million below year ago levels, according to data from Euroilstock Foundation.
The American Petroleum Institute said U.S. distillate inventories last week rose a modest 235,000 barrels to 112.1 million, still a sharp 21.5 million below a year ago.
